claim: Grasshoppers jumped in response to 57% of black (OFF) looming stimuli.
source: Grasshoppers jumped in response to all looming stimuli, escaping from 57% of black (OFF) looms and 45% of white (ON) looms (p=0.065; Figure 1B).
evidence: Behavioral data from experiments with looming stimuli of different contrast polarities.

claim: Grasshoppers jumped in response to 45% of white (ON) looming stimuli.
source: Grasshoppers jumped in response to all looming stimuli, escaping from 57% of black (OFF) looms and 45% of white (ON) looms (p=0.065; Figure 1B).
evidence: Behavioral data from experiments with looming stimuli of different contrast polarities.

claim: Jump probabilities were higher for OFF looms in six of the seven animals tested (p=0.047).
source: Jump probabilities were higher for OFF looms in six of the seven animals tested (p=0.047; Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data across individual animals.

claim: White stimuli produced earlier jumps for intermediate approach speeds (l/|v| of 80 ms) with a median jump time 223 ms earlier than black stimuli (p=8.9 • 10–4).
source: Specifically, for looming stimuli with an l/|v| of 80 ms the median jump time was 223 ms earlier (p=8.9 • 10–4); the jump time was also earlier, but not significantly so for white looms with an l/|v| of 40 or 120 ms.
evidence: Behavioral timing data from experiments with different approach speeds.

claim: The LGMD has a large distal dendritic field (field A) and two smaller ones more proximal to the SIZ (fields B and C).
source: The LGMD has a large distal dendritic field (field A) and two smaller ones more proximal to the SIZ (fields B and C; Figure 2A).
evidence: Anatomical description of the LGMD neuron structure.

claim: OFF inhibitory inputs impinge on dendritic field C of the LGMD.
source: Inhibitory inputs to the LGMD arise from pathways segregated by contrast polarity, with OFF inhibition impinging on dendritic field C and ON inhibition impinging on field B (Fraser Rowell et al., 1977; Strausfeld and Nässel, 1981).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD inhibitory pathways.

claim: ON inhibitory inputs impinge on dendritic field B of the LGMD.
source: Inhibitory inputs to the LGMD arise from pathways segregated by contrast polarity, with OFF inhibition impinging on dendritic field C and ON inhibition impinging on field B (Fraser Rowell et al., 1977; Strausfeld and Nässel, 1981).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD inhibitory pathways.

claim: Presentation of an OFF-looming stimulus produced an increase in fluorescence in field A.
source: Presentation of an OFF-looming stimulus produced the expected increase in fluorescence in field A (Figure 2B).
evidence: Calcium imaging data showing fluorescence changes in response to OFF stimuli.

claim: In response to an ON-looming stimulus, fluorescence increased in field C more than in field A.
source: In response to an ON-looming stimulus, however, fluorescence increased in field C more than in field A (Figure 2C, Video 2).
evidence: Calcium imaging data showing differential fluorescence changes in response to ON stimuli.

claim: No fluorescence changes were observed in field B, regardless of stimulus contrast polarity.
source: No fluorescence changes were observed in field B, regardless of stimulus contrast polarity.
evidence: Calcium imaging data showing absence of fluorescence changes in field B.

claim: ON looms produced field C responses 2.4 ± 1.2 times that of OFF looms.
source: ON looms produced field C responses 2.4 ± 1.2 times that of OFF looms, while in field A OFF loom responses were 3.6 ± 1.1 times those of ON looms (mean ± SD).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of calcium fluorescence responses across animals.

claim: In field A, OFF loom responses were 3.6 ± 1.1 times those of ON looms.
source: ON looms produced field C responses 2.4 ± 1.2 times that of OFF looms, while in field A OFF loom responses were 3.6 ± 1.1 times those of ON looms (mean ± SD).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of calcium fluorescence responses across animals.

claim: Direct iontophoresis of acetylcholine (ACh) to field C dendrites increased calcium fluorescence at the location of ACh application dependent on the amount of applied ACh.
source: Direct iontophoresis of acetylcholine (ACh) to field C dendrites increased calcium fluorescence at the location of ACh application dependent on the amount of applied ACh (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing dose-dependent response to ACh application.

claim: Local puffing of mecamylamine near field C reduced calcium fluorescence produced by looming stimuli within field C and at the SIZ.
source: Local puffing of mecamylamine near field C reduced calcium fluorescence produced by looming stimuli within field C and at the SIZ (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing effect of nAChR antagonist on calcium responses.

claim: Mecamylamine reduced peak dF/F in field C by 80 ± 8.5% for ON looms and 75 ± 17% for OFF looms.
source: Mecamylamine reduced peak dF/F in field C by 80 ± 8.5% for ON looms and 75 ± 17% for OFF looms (mean ± SD).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mecamylamine effect on calcium responses.

claim: Both ON and OFF looming stimuli produced synchronous activation of field C dendrites.
source: Both ON and OFF looming stimuli produced synchronous activation of field C dendrites (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: Temporal analysis of calcium imaging data across field C subregions.

claim: Field A exhibits sequential activation of dendritic regions as the loom expands.
source: This differs from field A, which exhibits sequential activation of dendritic regions as the loom expands (Figure 4D; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Temporal analysis of calcium imaging data across field A subregions, with reference to previous work.

claim: For 12 of 18 animals, all field C subregions had the same dF/F peak time in response to ON looms.
source: For 12 of 18 animals, all field C subregions had the same dF/F peak time in response to ON looms, and in no experiment did the responses suggest a retinotopic mapping of inputs to field C.
evidence: Statistical analysis of peak timing across animals and field C subregions.

claim: In no experiment did the responses suggest a retinotopic mapping of inputs to field C.
source: For 12 of 18 animals, all field C subregions had the same dF/F peak time in response to ON looms, and in no experiment did the responses suggest a retinotopic mapping of inputs to field C.
evidence: Analysis of spatial patterns of activation in field C.

claim: For field A, the CoM of dF/F moved across the dendritic arbor as the stimulus traversed the visual field.
source: For field A, the CoM of dF/F moved across the dendritic arbor as the stimulus traversed the visual field (Figure 4, blue lines).
evidence: Center of mass analysis of calcium responses during translating stimuli.

claim: For all trials tested in field A, the CoM position was correlated to stimulus position (p<0.001).
source: For all trials tested, the CoM position was correlated to stimulus position (p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between center of mass and stimulus position in field A.

claim: For field C, 9 of 21 trials had significant correlations between stimulus position and response CoM, but the CoM trajectories were short, winding, and inconsistent across trials within the same animal.
source: For field C, 9 of 21 trials had significant correlations between stimulus position and response CoM, but the CoM trajectories were short, winding, and inconsistent across trials within the same animal (Figure 4H, red lines).
evidence: Center of mass analysis showing lack of consistent retinotopic mapping in field C.

claim: A 80° change in stimulus position produced a mean shift in CoM of 3.5 ± 5.6 µm in one dimension and 1.6 ± 5.0 µm in the second dimension within field C.
source: A 80° change in stimulus position produced a mean shift in CoM of 3.5 ± 5.6 µm (mean ± SD) in one dimension and 1.6 ± 5.0 µm in the second dimension within field C (Figure 4H, right).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of center of mass displacement in field C.

claim: The same change in stimulus position resulted in a mean shift in CoM of 64.5 ± 25.8 µm and 84.3 ± 31 µm for the respective axes in field A.
source: In comparison, the same change in stimulus position resulted in a mean shift in CoM of 64.5 ± 25.8 µm and 84.3 ± 31 µm for the respective axes in field A.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of center of mass displacement in field A.

claim: The peak firing rate of the LGMD did not change with the spatial coherence of white looms.
source: Indeed, and in contrast to black looms, the peak firing rate of the LGMD did not change with the spatial coherence of white looms.
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing lack of coherence selectivity for white stimuli.

claim: The responses during the last second before collision contained more bursts for incoherent white looms.
source: However, the responses during the last second before collision contained more bursts for incoherent looms, a change in firing previously found to decrease escape responses for black looms (Figure 5B; Dewell and Gabbiani, 2018a).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing increased bursting for incoherent white stimuli.

claim: For spatially coherent stimuli, the peak firing rate for checkered stimuli was higher and occurred later than for solid white stimuli (p=0.001, sign-rank test).
source: For spatially coherent stimuli, the peak firing rate for checkered stimuli was higher and occurred later than for solid white stimuli (p=0.001, sign-rank test).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings comparing responses to checkered and white stimuli.

claim: Reducing the coherence of black and white checkered looming stimuli decreased LGMD firing.
source: Reducing the coherence of black and white checkered looming stimuli decreased LGMD firing (Figure 5C), as observed for solid black looms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing coherence selectivity for checkered stimuli.

claim: Of the nine animals studied, only three responded maximally to the 100% coherent stimulus for white looms.
source: Of the nine animals studied, only three responded maximally to the 100% coherent stimulus for white looms (Figure 5D), while all nine animals responded maximally to the 100% coherent stimulus for checkered looms (Figure 5E).
evidence: Analysis of individual animal responses to stimuli of varying coherence.

claim: All nine animals responded maximally to the 100% coherent stimulus for checkered looms.
source: Of the nine animals studied, only three responded maximally to the 100% coherent stimulus for white looms (Figure 5D), while all nine animals responded maximally to the 100% coherent stimulus for checkered looms (Figure 5E).
evidence: Analysis of individual animal responses to stimuli of varying coherence.

claim: The peak calcium fluorescence in field C was unchanged by the spatial coherence of ON looms.
source: The peak calcium fluorescence in field C was also unchanged by the spatial coherence of ON looms (Figure 5F).
evidence: Calcium imaging data showing lack of coherence selectivity in field C.

claim: The jump probability showed a slight decrease with reduced spatial coherence for white stimuli, but nothing like the steep coherence preference seen previously for black looming stimuli.
source: The jump probability showed a slight decrease with reduced spatial coherence, but nothing like the steep coherence preference seen previously for black looming stimuli (Figure 5G, Video 1 and Video 8).
evidence: Behavioral data comparing coherence selectivity for white and black stimuli.

claim: The dF/F was higher in field A than in field C during approach for both concentric squares and checkerboard stimuli.
source: The dF/F was higher in field A than in field C during approach for both stimuli and the post-loom flash response was higher in field C (Figure 6C and D), similar to the responses for solid black squares on a white background (Figure 2F).
evidence: Calcium imaging data comparing responses to mixed ON/OFF stimuli.

claim: For the seven animals tested, there was no difference in peak response between concentric squares, checkerboards, and OFF stimuli in either dendritic field.
source: For the seven animals tested, there was no difference in peak response between concentric squares, checkerboards, and OFF stimuli in either dendritic field (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Statistical analysis of calcium responses across different stimulus types.

claim: The response at the SIZ showed no preference for ON, OFF, or mixed stimuli indicating similar spiking output from all four tested stimuli.
source: The response at the SIZ showed no preference for ON, OFF, or mixed stimuli indicating similar spiking output from all four tested stimuli (Figure 6G).
evidence: Calcium imaging data at the spike initiation zone showing similar responses across stimulus types.

claim: Moving the excitatory inputs from field A to C produced higher firing in the model.
source: Excitation to field A generated by a simulated black loom produced reliable firing (Figure 7A and B, blue). Moving the excitatory inputs from field A to C produced higher firing (Figure 7B, dark red).
evidence: Computational modeling results showing effect of input location on firing.

claim: Reducing the number of field C excitatory synapses by 60% without changing the amount of inhibition still produced as much firing as the field A excitation simulation.
source: Reducing the number of field C excitatory synapses by 60% without changing the amount of inhibition still produced as much firing as the field A excitation simulation.
evidence: Computational modeling results showing efficiency of field C inputs.

claim: The more evenly the inputs were split between the fields, the larger the resulting neural response was.
source: The more evenly the inputs were split between the fields, the larger the resulting neural response was (Figure 7C).
evidence: Computational modeling results showing effect of input distribution on response magnitude.

claim: Looming excitation in field C with a similar spatial extent as that of field A reduced firing by 15%.
source: We found that looming excitation in field C with a similar spatial extent as that of field A reduced firing by 15% (Figure 7D).
evidence: Computational modeling results comparing random vs. clustered input mapping.

claim: The model reproduced the decreased firing and increased bursting of spatially incoherent stimuli seen in experimental data.
source: The model reproduced the decreased firing and increased bursting of spatially incoherent stimuli seen in experimental data (Figure 7E).
evidence: Computational modeling results validated against experimental data.

claim: ON excitation impinging onto field C produces energetic savings compared to the previously hypothesized retinotopic mapping to field A.
source: Based on these simulation results, ON excitation impinging onto field C produces energetic savings compared to the previously hypothesized retinotopic mapping to field A.
evidence: Inference from computational modeling results about energetic efficiency.

claim: Considering the 60% reduction in excitatory inputs to field C due to their proximity to the SIZ, this represents a 30% total input reduction without losing sensitivity to spatial coherence for textured stimuli.
source: Considering the 60% reduction in excitatory inputs to field C due to their proximity to the SIZ, this represents a 30% total input reduction without losing sensitivity to spatial coherence for textured stimuli.
evidence: Calculation based on modeling results about energetic savings.

claim: The LGMD receives retinotopic medullary excitation from columnar projections to dendritic field A through the second, crossed optic chiasm.
source: The LGMD receives retinotopic medullary excitation from columnar projections to dendritic field A through the second, crossed optic chiasm (Strausfeld and Nässel, 1981; Peron et al., 2009; Zhu and Gabbiani, 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Dendritic fields B and C receive non-retinotopic ON and OFF inhibition, respectively.
source: Dendritic fields B and C receive non-retinotopic ON and OFF inhibition, respectively (Fraser Rowell et al., 1977; Strausfeld and Nässel, 1981).
evidence: Referenced from previous anatomical studies.

claim: The DUB that projects to field C contains ~500 neurons with ~10° receptive fields impinging non-retinotopically to dendritic field C.
source: The projections to field C arise from the dorsal uncrossed bundle (DUB), which contains a subpopulation of ~500 neurons with ~10° receptive fields impinging non-retinotopically to dendritic field C (Gouranton, 1964; Strausfeld and Nässel, 1981; Elphick et al., 1996).
evidence: Referenced from previous anatomical studies.

claim: The OFF inhibitory inputs to field C have wider receptive fields (~50°) and only a small subset of the DUB axons likely encodes this inhibitory signal.
source: More recent work has shown that the OFF inhibitory inputs to field C have wider receptive fields (~50°) and that only a small subset of the DUB axons likely encodes this inhibitory signal, raising the possibility that the DUB contains more than one type of projection to field C (Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: Referenced from recent physiological studies.

claim: The LGMD distinguishes the coherence of dark (OFF) approaching objects through a retinotopic mapping of synaptic inputs onto compartmentalized field A dendrites and through intracellular processing by differentially distributed active conductances.
source: The LGMD distinguishes the coherence of dark (OFF) approaching objects through a retinotopic mapping of synaptic inputs onto compartmentalized field A dendrites and through intracellular processing by differentially distributed active conductances (Dewell and Gabbiani, 2018a; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD processing mechanisms.

claim: The LGMD contains an H-conductance and an inactivating K+ conductance localized in dendrites, as well as calcium and calcium-sensitive K+ conductances localized close to the spike initiation zone, and an M-type K+ conductance presumably localized in the axon.
source: These include an H-conductance and an inactivating K+ conductance localized in dendrites, as well as calcium and calcium-sensitive K+ conductances localized close to the spike initiation zone (SIZ), and an M-type K+ conductance presumably localized in the axon (Peron and Gabbiani, 2009; Dewell and Gabbiani, 2018a; Dewell and Gabbiani, 2018b).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies characterizing LGMD membrane conductances.

claim: The LGMD's excitatory inputs were believed to be processed independent of polarity, with both ON and OFF pathways projecting retinotopically to field A.
source: The LGMD's excitatory inputs, however, were believed to be processed independent of polarity, with both ON and OFF pathways projecting retinotopically to field A (Figure 1Ai, Figure 2A, colored dots; O'Shea and Rowell, 1976).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD excitatory inputs.

claim: The retinotopic arrangement of OFF inputs to field A has been documented, but not for ON stimuli.
source: This arrangement has been documented for OFF, but not for ON stimuli (Peron et al., 2009; Zhu and Gabbiani, 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies showing gap in knowledge about ON inputs.

claim: The previously described excitatory synaptic inputs onto field A are mediated through nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) channels that are calcium permeable.
source: The previously described excitatory synaptic inputs onto field A are mediated through nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) channels that are calcium permeable (Peron et al., 2009).
evidence: Referenced from previous pharmacological studies.

claim: The dendrites lack voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, which allows direct imaging of synaptic activation with an intracellularly injected fluorescent calcium dye.
source: As the dendrites lack voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, this allows direct imaging of synaptic activation with an intracellularly injected fluorescent calcium dye, while voltage-gated Ca2+ channels near the SIZ allow imaging of the neuron's SIZ activation (Peron and Gabbiani, 2009; Peron et al., 2009).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD membrane properties and imaging methods.

claim: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels near the SIZ allow imaging of the neuron's SIZ activation.
source: As the dendrites lack voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, this allows direct imaging of synaptic activation with an intracellularly injected fluorescent calcium dye, while voltage-gated Ca2+ channels near the SIZ allow imaging of the neuron's SIZ activation (Peron and Gabbiani, 2009; Peron et al., 2009).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD membrane properties and imaging methods.

claim: Mice and house flies escape more often from simulated black approaching stimuli.
source: In comparison, there has been little investigation into how behavior depends on contrast polarity although mice and house flies escape more often from simulated black approaching stimuli (Holmqvist and Srinivasan, 1991; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: Referenced from previous behavioral studies in other species.

claim: The visual world contains more information in luminance decreases, particularly for smaller, faster objects.
source: The visual world contains more information in luminance decreases, particularly for smaller, faster objects (Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Clark et al., 2014; Leonhardt et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on natural scene statistics.

claim: The LGMD is about as large as a human cerebellar Purkinje cell.
source: This so-called lobula giant movement detector (LGMD) neuron receives visual information from all ommatidia (facets) of the ipsilateral compound eye after processing in two intermediate neuropils. It is about as large as a human cerebellar Purkinje cell and its output is faithfully relayed by a second neuron, the descending contralateral movement detector (DCMD), to the cells coordinating escape jumps (O'Shea and Williams, 1974).
evidence: Comparison of LGMD size to mammalian neuron.

claim: The LGMD's output is faithfully relayed by the DCMD to the cells coordinating escape jumps.
source: It is about as large as a human cerebellar Purkinje cell and its output is faithfully relayed by a second neuron, the descending contralateral movement detector (DCMD), to the cells coordinating escape jumps (O'Shea and Williams, 1974).
evidence: Referenced from previous anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: The nervous system is an energetically expensive organ, estimated to consume over 20% of calories in humans.
source: The nervous system is an energetically expensive organ, estimated to consume over 20% of calories in humans.
evidence: General knowledge about brain energy consumption.

claim: Excitatory synaptic transmission contributes greatly to neuronal energetic cost, accounting for about 2/3 of the brain's total ATP consumption.
source: Excitatory synaptic transmission contributes greatly to this energetic cost, accounting for about 2/3 of the brain's total ATP consumption (Sibson et al., 1998; Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Niven, 2016; Zhukov et al., 2019).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on brain energy metabolism.

claim: Most of the energetic expense of synaptic transmission comes from the pumping of Na+ and Ca2+ ions out of neurons following excitatory synaptic events.
source: Most of that expense comes from the pumping of Na+ and Ca2+ ions out of neurons following excitatory synaptic events (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Hasenstaub et al., 2010).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on synaptic energy costs.

claim: The model EPSPs carried an average charge of 0.34 pC.
source: The model EPSPs carried an average charge of 0.34 pC (see 'Methods').
evidence: Calculation from computational model parameters.

claim: A simulated black loom had 80,000 EPSPs within field A, for a total charge of 27 nC or 1.7 • 1011 ions.
source: A simulated black loom had 80,000 EPSPs within field A, for a total charge of 27 nC or 1.7 • 1011 ions (after multiplication by Avogadro's number and division by Faraday's constant).
evidence: Calculation from computational model simulations.

claim: The final estimate of energetic expense of a loom with all excitation impinging on field A is 6 • 1010 ATP molecules.
source: Accounting for the efficiency of the Na/Ca exchanger (one Ca2+ ion per ATP molecule), our final estimate of energetic expense of a loom with all excitation impinging on field A is 6 • 1010 ATP molecules.
evidence: Calculation based on model data and known ion pump stoichiometry.

claim: Moving all inputs from field A to field C allows a 60% reduction in excitation while generating the same output, corresponding to a savings of 3.6 • 1010 ATP molecules per loom.
source: Modeling showed that moving all inputs from field A to field C allows a 60% reduction in excitation while generating the same output (Figure 7), corresponding to a savings 3.6 • 1010 ATP molecules per loom if all excitation impinged on field C and half that for split excitation.
evidence: Calculation based on modeling results about energetic savings.

claim: The estimate of ATP expenses was confirmed using two alternative ways of calculation.
source: The estimate of ATP expenses was confirmed using two alternative ways of calculation (see 'Methods').
evidence: Multiple calculation methods used to validate energy estimates.

claim: The energetic savings from moving excitation to field C are due to field C inputs impinging closer to the site of spike initiation.
source: These energetic savings are due to field C inputs impinging closer to the site of spike initiation.
evidence: Inference from modeling results about mechanism of energy savings.

claim: The ON inputs likely comprise fewer neurons, so the energetic savings from moving some excitation to field C are likely higher than estimated.
source: As the ON inputs likely comprise fewer neurons, the energetic savings from moving some excitation to field C are likely higher than estimated here.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical considerations about presynaptic circuitry.

claim: The LGMD2 has a dendritic field A of the same size and shape as that of the LGMD but lacks analogous fields B or C.
source: The LGMD2 has a dendritic field A of the same size and shape as that of the LGMD but lacks analogous fields B or C.
evidence: Anatomical comparison between LGMD and LGMD2 neurons.

claim: The LGMD2 responds with a strong preference to dark objects and exhibits limited ability to detect white approaching stimuli.
source: It responds with a strong preference to dark objects and exhibits limited ability to detect white approaching stimuli (Simmons and Rind, 1997; Rind and Leitinger, 2000).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD2 response properties.

claim: In both insects and mammals, the OFF pathway is more sensitive to fast movement than the ON pathway.
source: In both insects and mammals, the OFF pathway is more sensitive to fast movement than the ON pathway (Leonhardt et al., 2016; Mazade et al., 2019).
evidence: Referenced from previous comparative studies on ON/OFF pathways.

claim: In mammals, OFF neurons are biased toward central vision.
source: In mammals OFF neurons are biased toward central vision (Mulholland and Smith, 2021; Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on mammalian visual system organization.

claim: In the grasshopper, the excitatory OFF inputs to field A of the LGMD have the same spatial resolution as the eye (~2°).
source: In the grasshopper, the excitatory OFF inputs to field A of the LGMD have the same spatial resolution as the eye (~2°; Jones and Gabbiani, 2010).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on LGMD input resolution.

claim: Feedforward inhibitory inputs to field C have lower resolution with receptive fields tenfold larger than field A inputs.
source: Feedforward inhibitory inputs to field C have lower resolution with receptive fields tenfold larger (Wang et al., 2018a; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on field C inhibitory inputs.

claim: The known anatomy and current data suggest on the order of 15 times fewer presynaptic neurons with larger receptive fields than in field A project to field C.
source: The known anatomy and current data suggest on the order of 15 times fewer presynaptic neurons with larger receptive fields than in field A (Elphick et al., 1996; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on anatomical data and current findings.

claim: The DUB neurons are likely conveying the ON excitation to field C.
source: Since inhibitory input is conveyed by a small set of neurons with larger receptive fields (Wang et al., 2018a), these DUB neurons are likely conveying the ON excitation described herein.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical and physiological data.

claim: Inhibition during a looming stimulus is thought to act mainly through shunting of the membrane resistance.
source: Inhibition during a looming stimulus is thought to act mainly through shunting of the membrane resistance.
evidence: General knowledge about inhibitory mechanisms in neurons.

claim: Pharmacological block of field C inhibition showed that it mostly influences firing at the end of a loom when it causes the LGMD to stop firing.
source: Further, pharmacological block of field C inhibition showed that it mostly influences firing at the end of a loom when it causes the LGMD to stop firing (Gabbiani et al., 2002; Gabbiani et al., 2005).
evidence: Referenced from previous pharmacological studies.

claim: The termination of firing by field C inhibition is thought to be important for triggering escape.
source: This termination of firing is thought to be important for triggering escape (Fotowat et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from previous behavioral studies.

claim: The behavioral timing and coherence selectivity both match LGMD response changes, suggesting that the LGMD is initiating the jump escapes from both white and black looms.
source: That the behavioral timing and coherence selectivity both match LGMD response changes suggests that the LGMD is initiating the jump escapes from both white and black looms.
evidence: Inference based on correlation between neural and behavioral data.

claim: The reduced ability to discriminate the spatial coherence of an approaching white stimulus is presumably due to the excitatory ON inputs impinging non-retinotopically onto field C and a lack of HCN conductances devoted to processing them there.
source: Thus, this reduced ability to discriminate the spatial coherence of an approaching white stimulus is presumably due to the excitatory ON inputs impinging non-retinotopically onto field C and a lack of HCN conductances devoted to processing them there (Figure 4).
evidence: Inference based on anatomical and physiological findings.

claim: The coarser mapping and processing of ON stimuli has a minimal impact on detecting mixed ON/OFF stimuli, while reducing the total energetic cost of the circuit.
source: The coarser mapping and processing of ON stimuli thus has a minimal impact, while reducing the total energetic cost of the circuit.
evidence: Inference from experimental and modeling results about functional consequences.

claim: The differences in ON/OFF neuronal processing are behaviorally relevant, being tightly correlated with the animal's escape behavior to light and dark stimuli of variable coherence.
source: Further, we show that these differences in ON/OFF neuronal processing are behaviorally relevant, being tightly correlated with the animal's escape behavior to light and dark stimuli of variable coherence.
evidence: Correlation between neural processing differences and behavioral outcomes.

claim: The synaptic mapping of excitatory inputs affects the fine stimulus discrimination ability of single neurons.
source: Our results show that the synaptic mapping of excitatory inputs affects the fine stimulus discrimination ability of single neurons and document the resulting functional impact on behavior.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings about structure-function relationships.

claim: Evolution presumably settles on solutions that trend towards minimizing energy expenditure while maintaining required processing abilities.
source: Evolution presumably settles on solutions that trend towards minimizing energy expenditure while maintaining required processing abilities.
evidence: General principle about evolutionary optimization.

claim: Individual neurons process information by discriminating between patterns of synaptic inputs impinging on their dendrites.
source: Individual neurons process information by discriminating between patterns of synaptic inputs impinging on their dendrites.
evidence: General principle of neuronal computation.

claim: Presynaptic targeting, dendritic morphology, compartmentalization, and active membrane properties all shape neuronal processing.
source: Presynaptic targeting, dendritic morphology, compartmentalization, and active membrane properties all shape neuronal processing (London and Häusser, 2005; Major et al., 2013; Lefebvre et al., 2015; Hawkins and Ahmad, 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous reviews on dendritic computation.

claim: Many neurons, including pyramidal neurons, have distinct dendritic subfields proximal and distal to the site of spike initiation that receive functionally segregated synaptic inputs processed by distinct membrane conductances.
source: Many neurons, including the principal excitatory neurons of the mammalian cortex, pyramidal neurons, have distinct dendritic subfields proximal and distal to the site of spike initiation that receive functionally segregated synaptic inputs processed by distinct membrane conductances (Behabadi et al., 2012; Major et al., 2013; Hawkins and Ahmad, 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on pyramidal neuron organization.

claim: In the visual system, neural channels transmitting information about luminance increases (ON) and decreases (OFF) constitute one key example of parallel pathways requiring integration.
source: In the visual system, neural channels transmitting information about luminance increases (ON) and decreases (OFF) constitute one key example of parallel pathways requiring integration (Chen et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on visual processing.

claim: Luminance information is largely segregated between ON and OFF cells early on in the retina of mammals and in insect visual neuropils.
source: Although luminance information is largely segregated between ON and OFF cells early on in the retina of mammals and in insect visual neuropils, real-world scenes involve a mix of both (Leonhardt et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Mazade et al., 2019; Mulholland and Smith, 2021).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on early visual processing.

claim: Real-world scenes involve a mix of both ON and OFF information.
source: Although luminance information is largely segregated between ON and OFF cells early on in the retina of mammals and in insect visual neuropils, real-world scenes involve a mix of both (Leonhardt et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Mazade et al., 2019; Mulholland and Smith, 2021).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on natural scene statistics.

claim: It is likely that approaching predators contain more OFF than ON information.
source: Although the contrast statistics of approaching predators has not been determined, it is likely that they also contain more OFF than ON information (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculation based on general visual statistics and referenced study.

claim: The LGMD neuron receives visual information from all ommatidia (facets) of the ipsilateral compound eye after processing in two intermediate neuropils.
source: This so-called lobula giant movement detector (LGMD) neuron receives visual information from all ommatidia (facets) of the ipsilateral compound eye after processing in two intermediate neuropils.
evidence: Anatomical description of LGMD inputs.

claim: Dendritic field C arborizes in a distinct sub-compartment of the lobula, called the dorsal lobula.
source: In particular, dendritic field C arborizes in a distinct sub-compartment of the lobula, called the dorsal lobula (O'Shea and Williams, 1974; Rosner et al., 2017).
evidence: Referenced from previous anatomical studies.

claim: In mammals and insects, visual processing is similarly split between ON and OFF pathways.
source: In mammals and insects, visual processing is similarly split between ON and OFF pathways.
evidence: General comparative statement about visual processing.

claim: In both mammals and insects, photoreceptors respond to luminance changes of either polarity.
source: In both cases, photoreceptors respond to luminance changes of either polarity, but at the next stage increments and decrements are encoded by different neurons in the mammalian retina: the ON and OFF bipolar cell classes (Euler et al., 2014; Clark and Demb, 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on early visual processing.

claim: In the mammalian retina, luminance increments and decrements are encoded by different neurons at the bipolar cell stage: the ON and OFF bipolar cell classes.
source: In both cases, photoreceptors respond to luminance changes of either polarity, but at the next stage increments and decrements are encoded by different neurons in the mammalian retina: the ON and OFF bipolar cell classes (Euler et al., 2014; Clark and Demb, 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on retinal processing.

claim: In the lamina of the insect optic lobe, the large monopolar cells L1, L2, and L3 postsynaptic to photoreceptors respond differently to luminance and contrast changes of either polarity.
source: In the lamina of the insect optic lobe, the large monopolar cells L1, L2, and L3 postsynaptic to photoreceptors respond differently to luminance and contrast changes of either polarity and distribute this information to ON and OFF neuron classes downstream that become increasingly selective (Clark et al., 2011; Strother et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on insect visual processing.

claim: Large monopolar cells regulate contrast selectivity dynamically depending on background luminance levels.
source: Further, large monopolar cells regulate contrast selectivity dynamically depending on background luminance levels (Ketkar et al., 2020; Ketkar et al., 2022).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on adaptive visual processing.

claim: The similarities of contrast polarity encoding between taxa likely result from visual processing being tuned to the statistics of natural scenes.
source: The similarities of contrast polarity encoding between taxa likely result from visual processing being tuned to the statistics of natural scenes (Clark et al., 2014; Clark and Demb, 2016; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference about evolutionary convergence referenced from previous studies.

claim: Field A of the LGMD has ~131,000 excitatory synapses.
source: Field A of the LGMD has ~131,000 excitatory synapses (Rind et al., 2016) and our looming stimuli cover ~20% of the eye, suggesting Nsyn= 26,200.
evidence: Referenced from previous anatomical study.

claim: Past recordings of medulla neurons presynaptic to the LGMD found they fired ~40 spikes per loom.
source: Past recordings of medulla neurons presynaptic to the LGMD found they fired ~40 spikes per loom, so this estimate would be in good agreement with our modeling results (Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: Referenced from previous electrophysiological study.

claim: Within hippocampal pyramidal neurons, distal CA1 dendrites receive excitation from entorhinal cortex while proximal dendrites are excited by inputs from CA3.
source: Within hippocampal pyramidal neurons, distal CA1 dendrites receive excitation from entorhinal cortex while proximal dendrites are excited by inputs from CA3.
evidence: General knowledge about hippocampal circuit organization.

claim: Hippocampal dendritic regions have distinct sets of active channels.
source: These dendritic regions also have distinct sets of active channels (London and Häusser, 2005; Spruston, 2008; Lefebvre et al., 2015).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on hippocampal neuron biophysics.

claim: An alternative hypothesis suggests that proximal excitation is the primary driver of spiking while distal excitation is modulatory in pyramidal neurons.
source: An alternative hypothesis to that put forth above suggests that proximal excitation is the primary driver of spiking while distal excitation is modulatory (Behabadi et al., 2012; Hawkins and Ahmad, 2016).
evidence: Referenced from previous theoretical studies on dendritic integration.

claim: Active processing in distal dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons can produce fine discrimination of the spatiotemporal pattern of excitatory inputs.
source: Active processing in distal dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons can produce fine discrimination of the spatiotemporal pattern of excitatory inputs even if dendritic compartmentalization and the location-dependence of synaptic integration are variable (Poirazi and Papoutsi, 2020).
evidence: Referenced from previous computational studies on dendritic computation.

claim: Within cortex, feedback from higher cortical areas excites the distal apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons that also have increased active conductances.
source: Within cortex, feedback from higher cortical areas excites the distal apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons that also have increased active conductances that can produce fine discrimination of distal inputs (Schuman et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on cortical feedback pathways.

claim: It has been suggested that the dendritic segregation of feedforward and feedback cortical inputs might underlie the comparison of sensory (bottom-up) inputs with top-down predictions.
source: It has been suggested that the dendritic segregation of feedforward and feedback cortical inputs might underlie the comparison of sensory (bottom-up) inputs with top-down predictions (Larkum, 2013).
evidence: Referenced from previous theoretical work on predictive coding.

claim: Distal feedback inputs might allow a finer discrimination of top-down than proximal bottom-up inputs in cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: In this context, our work suggests that distal feedback inputs might allow a finer discrimination of top-down than proximal bottom-up inputs.
evidence: Inference from current findings applied to cortical processing.

claim: Mice have a stronger behavioral response to black looms and looming-sensitive neurons in the superior colliculus show a preference for OFF inputs.
source: Mice have a stronger behavioral response to black looms and looming-sensitive neurons in the superior colliculus show a preference for OFF inputs (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013; Branco and Redgrave, 2020).
evidence: Referenced from previous studies on mammalian looming detection.

claim: The combination of reduced energy cost of field C inputs with increased discrimination by active processing in field A suggests a possible general principle for dendritic mapping.
source: The combination of reduced energy cost of field C inputs with increased discrimination by active processing in field A suggests a possible general principle for dendritic mapping whereby finer discriminations of the synaptic input pattern are implemented in distal, active dendrites while coarser discriminations are implemented by proximal dendrites.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings proposing a general principle.

claim: Having excitatory inputs spread between dendritic regions offers energetic savings as concentrating inputs reduces the driving force of the activated receptor channels.
source: Additionally, having excitatory inputs spread between dendritic regions offers energetic savings of its own as concentrating inputs reduces the driving force of the activated receptor channels (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Inference from modeling results about biophysical mechanisms.
